A user thanked the project, saying the Appwrite community on Discord is very helpful and the self-hosting guide is great. They contrasted it with a 'terrible experience' with Supabase, which they felt cripples its self-hosted option.
A user said Supabase's self-hosted option was 'wack' when they tried it a few months earlier. After reading the comparison, they might give Appwrite a try.

A user felt they weren't the target market: the point of a BaaS for them is not having to maintain anything, so self-hosting defeats the purpose. They also asked for an always-on Docker container/web server compute model, arguing serverless functions mostly have downsides for non-hobby projects.
A user said they had 'kicked the tires' on Appwrite a year earlier and liked it, but didn't have a big need for it. They noted a lot of great features had been added since then.

A user evaluating Firebase and Supabase for a new project was about to give up and go back to Laravel. They said Appwrite looked 'very interesting' and might solve their problem, but asked whether it supports Postgres (it did not yet).

A user pointed to Appwrite's installation and production docs as something they would love to see in Supabase's docs. They described Supabase's guidance for running a self-hosted production instance as lacking by comparison.

A critical user listed several concerns. Appwrite is written in PHP, which they doubt is extensible or scalable. It had no Cloud version yet, so it wasn't really 'as a service'. It isn't built on Postgres. GraphQL progress was slow. Overall, they felt it moves slower than Supabase on the features they care about.

A user had watched Supabase for months without adopting it, but was 'instantly sold' on Appwrite. They called Supabase 'fancy UI and marketing' and said they could easily self-install Appwrite for home projects, which they couldn't do with Supabase. They said they'd pay Appwrite for commercial hosting.

A user argued that 'self-host your own BaaS' is an oxymoron. Installing Appwrite on a DigitalOcean droplet means it is no longer a backend-as-a-service, and developers who choose Firebase don't want to manage servers.
A user said they couldn't find any documentation on scaling, such as how Appwrite scales the WebSocket connection pool, workers, and cloud functions.
A user noted this was the first 'Firebase clone' they had seen that attempts to implement the Firestore database model.
A user who is usually wary of this kind of product said Appwrite looks awesome. They added that the polish and content of the website really helped convince them.

An early user, who had been trying a similar service called Base, said Base's offline development story was lacking. They liked that Appwrite provides a containerized setup, which should make distributed development and testing easier.

Several early commenters complained there was no information on architecture or tech stack. Their questions included which storage and database backends are used, how to scale or change them, and how to back up or connect to other data sources.
A commenter said Appwrite reminded them of Directus, another headless PHP REST API backend with an admin UI. They asked how Appwrite differs apart from its end-to-end encryption.

A non-affiliated user who has tracked Appwrite since launch called it a tough, crowded segment. They said these opinionated abstractions become limiting once you need flexibility or scale, though good open-source options are wanted and someone 'has to keep Supabase honest'.

On the Appwrite Sites launch, several users complained the thread was dominated by bot, employee, or astroturf comments posted without disclosing affiliation, calling it 'pretty scummy'. One said the spam was a footgun because the product itself looks worthwhile as an open-source alternative to Vercel.
